scenes.title: Picture constant acceleration

beats.text: Consider a trolley moving along a straight track. It is already moving, and gains the same amount of velocity each second.
Watch it cover more ground in equal times. Its acceleration is constant.
If those velocity gains changed, the acceleration would vary. These formulae would no longer describe the whole interval.
beats.caption: Constant acceleration is essential.

scenes.title: Derive velocity from gradient

beats.text: Now the velocity time graph: start at u, finish at v, after time t.
Choose right as positive. Acceleration a is constant. Displacement s is the signed area. Derive the final velocity.
Acceleration equals gradient: change in velocity divided by elapsed time.
The change in velocity is final minus initial: v minus u. The elapsed time is t.
Multiply both sides by t. That gives a t equals v minus u.
Add u. V equals u plus a t: initial velocity plus the change.
A constant gradient is why the graph is straight. This equation tells us how much the velocity changes.
beats.caption: Constant gradient gives a straight line.

scenes.title: Derive displacement from area

beats.text: Now find the displacement over the same interval. Keep the endpoint velocities and time on the graph.
Displacement equals signed area under the velocity time graph. Here that shape is a trapezium.
Trapezium area is half the sum of the parallel sides, multiplied by the perpendicular width.
The parallel sides are u and v. The width between them is t. The sloping edge is not a parallel side.
So displacement equals half u plus v, multiplied by t.
This is average velocity times time. If the graph goes below the time axis, that area contributes negative displacement.
beats.caption: Signed area gives displacement.

scenes.title: Remove final velocity

beats.text: Now create the other equations. First, remove final velocity.
Start with displacement equals half u plus v, times t.
Replace v with u plus a t from the gradient equation. Keep the brackets.
Collect the two u terms inside: half of two u plus a t, all multiplied by t.
Expand. Half times two u times t is u t. The other term is half a t squared.
Use this form when initial velocity, acceleration and time are known. You do not need final velocity.
beats.caption: No final velocity needed.

scenes.title: Remove initial velocity

beats.text: If final velocity is known instead, remove initial velocity.
Begin again with the trapezium result.
Rearrange v equals u plus a t: u equals v minus a t.
Substitute that expression for u.
Collect terms: half of two v minus a t, multiplied by t.
Expand to get v t minus half a t squared. The minus sign comes from replacing u by v minus a t.

scenes.title: Remove time

beats.text: To remove time, first assume acceleration is nonzero.
Begin with the area formula.
From v equals u plus a t, time equals v minus u divided by a.
Substitute that fraction for time in the area equation.
Multiply both sides by two a.
The product is a difference of squares: v squared minus u squared.
Add u squared. We obtain v squared equals u squared plus two a s.
If acceleration is zero, v equals u, so the final identity still holds. Only the division step required nonzero acceleration.
beats.caption: The final identity also covers a = 0.

scenes.title: Choose the equation you need

beats.text: Choose the equation that omits the quantity you do not need.
beats.caption: Choose by the quantity omitted.

beats.text: No displacement? Use v equals u plus a t.
No acceleration? Use the trapezium equation.
No final velocity? Use u t plus half a t squared.
No initial velocity? Use v t minus half a t squared.
Check: you know u, a and s. Find v without time. Which equation?
beats.caption: Which equation avoids finding time?
